questions.q: What is the main goal of the asymptotic analysis of an algorithm?
choices: To count the exact number of operations for one particular input
To understand how the amount of work grows as the input size grows
To measure the running time in seconds on a specific machine
To find the smallest input on which the algorithm fails
questions.explain: The goal is not an exact operation count. It is how the work grows as n grows, so we focus on the dominant growth.

questions.q: GenericSORT runs: for i ← 1 to n: for j ← i + 1 to n: if A[i] > A[j]: swap. For n = 5, how many times is the comparison A[i] > A[j] executed?
questions.explain: For each i the inner loop runs n − i times: 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 + 0 = 10. In general the count is n(n − 1)/2.

questions.q: GenericSORT (two nested loops: i from 1 to n, j from i + 1 to n) performs n(n − 1)/2 comparisons on every input. What is the tight bound on its number of comparisons?
questions.explain: n(n − 1)/2 = ½n^2 − ½n is a degree-2 polynomial, so it is Θ(n^2).

questions.q: If an algorithm runs quickly on small inputs, it will also be practical on very large inputs.
questions.explain: Two algorithms can solve the same problem with very different growth. One that is fine for small n can become impractical when n is very large.

questions.q: Which is the formal definition of T(n) = O(f(n))?
choices: There exist constants c and n0 such that T(n) ≤ c·f(n) for all n ≥ n0
There exist constants c and n0 such that T(n) ≥ c·f(n) for all n ≥ n0
T(n) = c·f(n) for some constant c
questions.explain: Big O needs some constant c and starting point n0 so that T(n) never exceeds c·f(n) once n ≥ n0. The ≥ version is the definition of Ω.

questions.q: For T(n) = O(f(n)) to hold, T(n) ≤ c·f(n) must be true for every input size n, including small ones.
questions.explain: Big O is an eventual upper bound. The inequality only has to hold for n ≥ n0. What happens for small n does not matter.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Big O is described as an eventual ______ bound.
questions.explain: T(n) stays at or below c·f(n) (upper bound) from n0 onward (eventual).

questions.q: Which of these statements are true?
questions.explain: n^2 ≤ n^3 for n ≥ 1, so a loose upper bound is valid. 5n^2 + 3n ≤ 8n^2 and 7n^4 + n ≤ 8n^4 for n ≥ 1. n^3 ≤ c·n^2 would need n ≤ c for all large n, which fails.

questions.q: The statement n^2 = O(n^3) is false, because n^3 is not a tight bound for n^2.
questions.explain: Big O is only an upper bound. It does not have to be tight. For n ≥ 1, n^2 ≤ 1·n^3, so n^2 = O(n^3) is true.

questions.q: Proposition 1 says that a polynomial of degree k is:
questions.explain: A polynomial a_k·n^k + ... + a_1·n + a_0 is O(n^k). It is not O(n^(k−1)) or any lower power.

questions.q: The proof of Proposition 1 picks n0 = 1 and c = the sum of the absolute values of the coefficients. What c does it pick for T(n) = 3n^3 − 2n^2 + n + 4?
questions.explain: c = |3| + |−2| + |1| + |4| = 3 + 2 + 1 + 4 = 10. The negative coefficient counts as +2.

questions.q: In the proof of Proposition 1, why is n0 chosen to be 1?
choices: For n ≥ 1, n^k is at least as large as every lower power of n, which is needed to replace every power with n^k
Because the definition of Big O requires n0 = 1
Because absolute values are only defined for n ≥ 1
questions.explain: The step that raises n^0, n^1, ..., n^(k−1) up to n^k only makes the right side bigger when n ≥ 1. For 0 < n < 1, higher powers are smaller.

questions.q: In the proof of Proposition 1, why can each coefficient a_i be replaced by |a_i| while keeping T(n) ≤ (the new expression)?
choices: Because |a| ≥ a for every real number a, so the expression can only stay the same or get larger
Because polynomial coefficients are always positive
Because taking absolute values makes the polynomial equal to c·n^k
Because Big O ignores negative coefficients
questions.explain: A number's absolute value is at least as large as the number (larger if it is negative). Raising the right side turns = into ≤.

questions.q: Compare 4x^2 + 2x + 1 with 7x^2. They are equal at x = 1, and for every x > 1, 7x^2 is the larger one.
questions.explain: At x = 1 both equal 7. 7x^2 − (4x^2 + 2x + 1) = 3x^2 − 2x − 1 = (3x + 1)(x − 1), which is positive for x > 1. So 4x^2 + 2x + 1 = O(x^2) with c = 7, n0 = 1.

questions.q: Which term determines the asymptotic growth of 12n^3 + n^2 + 100? (Write it like n^2.)
questions.explain: The highest-degree term, 12n^3, dominates. Its growth is n^3, and the coefficient 12 does not change that.

questions.q: T(n) = 5n^3 + 7n^2 + 3n + 10. Which is the best (lowest) Big O bound?
questions.explain: The highest-degree term is n^3. As n grows, 7n^2, 3n, and 10 become small compared with n^3.

questions.q: Changing the leading term of a polynomial from 5n^3 to 500n^3 changes its growth category.
questions.explain: Constant coefficients do not change the growth category. Both are Θ(n^3).

questions.q: Which function grows fastest as n becomes very large?
questions.explain: 0.001n^3 has the highest degree (3). Coefficients do not decide growth, so it eventually passes the degree-2 and degree-1 functions.

questions.q: For T(n) = ½n^3 + 3n, which of these are true?
questions.explain: The dominant term is n^3 (degree 3). Big O holds for powers ≥ 3, Ω holds for powers ≤ 3, and Θ holds only at exactly 3. So O(n) and O(n^2) are false and the rest are true.

questions.q: To disprove n^k = O(n^(k−1)), assume n^k ≤ c·n^(k−1) for all large n and divide both sides by n^(k−1). What do you get?
questions.explain: n^k / n^(k−1) = n, so the assumption becomes n ≤ c for all sufficiently large n.

questions.q: Why does the requirement "n ≤ c for all sufficiently large n" give a contradiction?
choices: n keeps growing and eventually passes any fixed constant c
c has to be an integer
questions.explain: No fixed constant can stay above n forever, so no c works and n^k ≠ O(n^(k−1)).

questions.q: The same divide-and-compare argument shows that n^5 is not O(n^2).
questions.explain: n^5 ≤ c·n^2 would mean n^3 ≤ c for all large n, which is impossible. A degree-k polynomial is not O(n^m) for any m < k.

questions.q: Suppose ½n^3 + 3n ≤ 10n^2 held for all large n. Then ½n^3 ≤ 10n^2 would hold too. Dividing by n^2, this requires n ≤ what number?
questions.explain: ½n ≤ 10, so n ≤ 20. That fails once n > 20, so ½n^3 + 3n is not bounded by 10n^2. The same happens for any c (n ≤ 2c), so it is not O(n^2).

questions.q: Which condition, for some constants c and n0 and all n ≥ n0, defines T(n) = Ω(f(n))?
questions.explain: Ω is a lower bound, the mirror image of Big O: ≤ becomes ≥. The two-sided version is Θ.

questions.q: Which of these statements are true?
questions.explain: n^3 ≥ n for n ≥ 1. 4n^2 + 2n ≥ 4n^2. ½n^3 + 3n ≥ ½n^3. But n ≥ c·n^2 and 10n^2 ≥ c·n^3 both fail for large n.

questions.q: To show 4n^2 + 2n = Ω(n^2), we need 4n^2 + 2n ≥ c·n^2 for all n ≥ 1. What is the largest constant c that works?
questions.explain: Dividing by n^2 gives 4 + 2/n ≥ c. 2/n gets close to 0 as n grows, so c = 4 works and anything above 4 eventually fails.

questions.q: Why is n NOT Ω(n^2)?
choices: n ≥ c·n^2 means 1 ≥ c·n, which fails once n > 1/c
n is smaller than n^2 when n = 1
Ω only applies to polynomials of degree 2 or more
n ≥ c·n^2 requires c to be negative
questions.explain: Dividing n ≥ c·n^2 by n gives 1 ≥ c·n. For any positive c, this breaks once n > 1/c, so no constant works for all large n.

questions.q: T(n) = Θ(f(n)) means T(n) is both O(f(n)) and Ω(f(n)).
questions.explain: c1·f(n) ≤ T(n) ≤ c2·f(n). The c2 side is the Big O bound and the c1 side is the Ω bound.

questions.q: Give the tight asymptotic bound of T(n) = 10n^2 + 7n + 4, in the form Θ(...).
questions.explain: The dominant term is 10n^2. For n ≥ 1: 10n^2 ≤ 10n^2 + 7n + 4 ≤ 21n^2, so c1 = 10, c2 = 21, n0 = 1.

questions.q: T(n) = 3n + 5 is Θ(n). Which choices of constants satisfy c1·n ≤ 3n + 5 ≤ c2·n for all n ≥ n0?
questions.explain: (3, 8, 1): 3n ≤ 3n + 5 ≤ 3n + 5n = 8n. (1, 4, 5): 3n + 5 ≤ 4n exactly when n ≥ 5. c1 = 4 fails for n > 5, c2 = 3 never works, and c2 = 4 fails at n = 1 (8 > 4).

questions.q: Because ½n^3 + 3n = Ω(n), it is also Θ(n).
questions.explain: Θ needs both bounds with the same f(n). ½n^3 + 3n is Ω(n) but not O(n), so it is not Θ(n). Its tight bound is Θ(n^3).

questions.q: Using the absolute-value-sum method with n0 = 1, what upper constant c2 gives ½n^3 + 3n ≤ c2·n^3?
questions.explain: For n ≥ 1, ½n^3 + 3n ≤ ½n^3 + 3n^3 = 3.5n^3. With c1 = ½ for the lower side, this shows Θ(n^3).
